Am I required to buy it?

Federal law requires it only in a high-risk zone (A or V) with a federally regulated or backed mortgage, or federal help to buy or build (42 U.S.C. §4012a). Outside those zones, a lender may still require it.

In Florida, a home insured by Citizens Property Insurance with wind coverage must also carry flood insurance. In a high-risk zone (A or V) this has applied since 2023 (new policies from April 1, renewals from July 1), whatever the home is worth. Outside those zones it phases in by rebuilding cost: from January 1, 2026 at $400,000 or more, and from January 1, 2027 for all other Citizens homes. Condo-unit and no-wind policies are exempt.

A private flood policy can meet a lender's flood requirement: federally regulated lenders must accept a private policy that meets the federal definition of private flood insurance and covers at least what the loan requires (12 CFR §339.3(c)). Its price is not in FEMA's records. Citizens does not sell flood insurance: the required flood policy comes from another insurer, the NFIP or a private one, and must at least match the NFIP's dwelling coverage or meet Florida's private flood insurance rules (s. 627.715).

At a closing: Where a federally regulated lender must require it, the legal minimum is the loan balance or the NFIP's limit for the property, whichever is less (42 U.S.C. §4012a(b)). If such a lender notifies you that coverage is needed and you do not buy it within 45 days, the lender must buy it for you and can charge you for it (42 U.S.C. §4012a(e)). If you think a lender's high-risk-zone finding is wrong, you and the lender together can ask FEMA to review it within 45 days of the lender's notice; a fee applies (44 CFR §65.17). Buying a finished home with an NFIP building policy: the seller can assign the policy to you in writing when title transfers. In Florida, a home seller must give the buyer a flood disclosure at or before the sales contract, saying whether the seller knows of flood damage during their ownership, filed a flood claim, or received flood aid (s. 689.302, F.S.).

58.8% of Sarasota County's NFIP policy units are in high-risk zones (not 58.8% of all buildings, and not an answer about your own home).

Flood map: FEMA's current flood map for unincorporated Sarasota County took effect March 27, 2024. FEMA's latest Community Status Book lists no new flood map taking effect for the towns and areas FEMA lists in this county; that does not cover maps still preliminary (below). FEMA's digital flood map for Sarasota County has 151 map panels, the oldest in effect since November 4, 2016 and the newest since March 27, 2024. FEMA has revised that map by 6 Letters of Map Revision, 6 of them in effect since January 1, 2021. FEMA's map service lists 2,051 rulings for owners here who asked FEMA to take a building or lot out of the high-risk zone (Letters of Map Amendment): 1,696 took the building or some or all of the lot out, 164 found it already outside the zone as mapped, 111 were denied, 80 other or mixed. FEMA charges no review or processing fee for a Letter of Map Amendment request (44 CFR §72.5). FEMA's Online LOMC site lets home owners or their representatives ask FEMA for a Letter of Map Change. Your home may already have an Elevation Certificate on file with your community: ask your local floodplain manager, often in the city or county building, permitting or engineering department. If none is on file, a land surveyor, engineer or architect completes one. These are rulings for owners who chose to apply, so they are not the odds for your home, and FEMA's map service gives no dates for them. They are counted by the towns and areas FEMA lists in this county, so a city that reaches into a neighboring county counts in full here. FEMA's preliminary flood map data give an early look at a home's or community's projected flood risk and may include new or revised flood maps. Check your own address on FEMA's flood map or with our flood zone map lookup by address.

How do I actually get covered — and how fast?

Most policies start 30 days after you buy. Bought while making, increasing, extending or renewing a mortgage, it can start at closing if the insurer is paid within 10 days (30 if the lender, title company or settlement attorney pays).

  • Waiting period30 days
  • Bought with a new or refinanced mortgageCan start at closing, if paid in time
  • NFIP building limit$250,000
  • NFIP contents limit$100,000

Most homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage. Exceptions in FEMA's flood insurance manual: with a loan secured by the insured property (making, increasing, extending or renewing it), coverage you apply for on or before closing can start at the time of the loan closing if the insurer gets the form and full amount due in time; the wait is one day when a FEMA map revision newly shows the building in a high-risk zone and the insurer gets them within 13 months of the revision's effective date. One more exception (44 CFR 61.11(c)): coverage starts the day after you apply and pay when FEMA determines the property is affected by flooding on federal land caused or made worse by post-wildfire conditions, and you buy it within 60 days after the fire's containment date. To buy: call the NFIP at (877) 336-2627, go to FloodSmart.gov, or ask any licensed insurance agent. Every NFIP insurer offers the same rates. The program nationwide: the NFIP in numbers.

Congress has to keep renewing the NFIP's authority. During a lapse, NFIP policies cannot be bought, renewed or increased until the authority returns. Policies already in force run to their expiration date and claims on them are still handled, though FEMA says the money to pay claims may be limited.

What it won't pay: The policy generally counts a flood only when water covers two or more acres of normally dry land or two or more properties, one of them yours. The NFIP's standard policy for homes (the Dwelling Form) does not pay for a hotel or other living costs while you are out of the home, or for belongings outside the building, and it limits what it pays for in a basement. Belongings are paid at actual cash value (their used value), not the cost of new ones. Hurricanes can cause both wind and flood damage. A standard NFIP policy does not pay for wind damage, including rain blown in by wind or water coming through a roof the wind damaged; it does pay for water entering from the ground up, such as storm surge. Other policies, such as homeowners policies, may cover wind-driven rain, so you will likely file claims with both.

Already flooded? Insured: report the loss to your insurance agent or company now (FEMA's steps: how to start a flood claim), and send a proof of loss (your signed, sworn statement of the amount you are claiming) within 60 days of the flood (44 CFR 61, App. A(1), Art. VII). Not insured: a policy bought today will not cover a flood that already happened, and FEMA disaster aid is open to people in counties designated in a federally declared disaster. If FEMA aid after a flood goes to buy or build a home in a high-risk zone, you must buy and keep flood insurance on it for at least the amount of the aid, or you cannot get federal aid for later flood damage to it (44 CFR §206.110).

NFIP claim denied? You can appeal to FEMA within 60 days of the date on the denial letter, and you can sue within one year of the denial. An appeal does not extend that year. Under the NFIP's rules, a building is substantially damaged when restoring it to its condition before the damage would cost 50 percent or more of its market value before the damage (44 CFR §59.1). An NFIP policy with building coverage pays up to $30,000 under Increased Cost of Compliance to comply with a state or local floodplain law when repairing a flood-damaged building.

Your state's insurance regulator: Florida Department of Financial Services (consumer help).

Source: floodsmart.gov, agents.floodsmart.gov, ecfr.gov, law.cornell.edu, fema.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

Would a policy here pay to rebuild my home?

Not in full for at least 53.3% of the 12,167 single-family policies here that report a rebuilding cost: FEMA's records put it above the NFIP's $250,000 building limit.

  • Rebuilding cost above the building limit (of 12,167 policies reporting one)53.3%Florida: 38.5%
  • Single-family policies insured to the building maximum (all of them, not only those above)89.7%
  • Damage was more than the coverage (of 9,578 claims paid with a damage figure)5.1%

The two shares have different bases: insured-to-the-maximum counts every single-family policy with the full building limit; the rebuilding-cost share counts only the policies that report a rebuilding cost. Homes insured for less than their own rebuilding cost can also fall short. How this is counted

The NFIP pays the cost to rebuild (not a depreciated value) only for a single-family home that is your principal residence and is insured for at least 80% of its full rebuilding cost, or for the $250,000 maximum.

What the zone codes mean (44 CFR §64.3): A, AE and A1–A30 are high-risk; AO and AH are high-risk with shallow flooding; A99 is high-risk behind a flood barrier FEMA treats as complete; V, VE and V1–V30 are coastal high-risk, flooded by tides with fast-moving water (velocity); B and X are areas of moderate flood hazard, C and X areas of minimal hazard; D has possible but undetermined flood hazards. A 1 percent or greater chance a year works out to a 26% or greater chance of at least one such flood over 30 years.

Why can a high-risk zone cost less than Zone X here? The premium is based on the flood risk of the building. The reason for any one zone is not in this data.

Zones with fewer than 50 priced single-family policies are omitted. Your own premium still depends on elevation and coverage.

How do current premiums compare with FEMA's full-risk price?

45.0% of single-family primary-home policies in Sarasota County have a premium below FEMA's full-risk premium, so those policies' bills are rising toward it. Median premium $860, full-risk $1,062 (premiums only, before fees).

  • Median premium charged (before fees)$860
  • Median full-risk premium$1,062
  • Pay below full-risk45.0% of 24,367Florida: 45.2%

Yearly cap: Except for the Emergency Program discount, statutory discounts gradually phase out through an annual increase cap discount at each renewal date until the policy reaches its full-risk premium. By law, most premium rates may not rise more than 18% a year; the rate for some property, including homes that are not a primary residence and business property, rises 25% a year until that group's average rate reaches the level the law sets (42 U.S.C. §4015(e)). FloodSmart puts the limit at 18 to 25% a year for most policyholders. It usually does not apply to new policies, raising your coverage or lowering your deductible can go past it, and fees and surcharges are added on top.

Paying a renewal 30 days or more after the policy expires causes a lapse in coverage. You then need a new application, and the lapse may cost you statutory discounts (what keeps a bill below full risk), including the yearly cap.

How much flood risk is here?

Relatively High for coastal flooding and Relatively High for inland (river) flooding, by FEMA's county rating. That compares this county with others; it is not a forecast for your address.

  • Coastal flood risk rating (FEMA)Relatively High
  • Inland flood risk rating (FEMA)Relatively High

FEMA's rating weighs modeled loss with social vulnerability and community resilience; it is not a prediction for your home, and it can differ from the loss percentile below. Coastal: FEMA models roughly $7.3 million of flood loss a year (buildings, people and farmland valued in dollars, insured or not; a model, not insurance payouts); a separate FEMA measure, loss per dollar of building value: coastal flood loss here is higher than in about 78% of U.S. counties. Inland: FEMA models roughly $67.2 million of flood loss a year (buildings, people and farmland valued in dollars, insured or not; a model, not insurance payouts); a separate FEMA measure, loss per dollar of building value: inland flood loss here is higher than in about 42% of U.S. counties. Loss figures model all flood loss, insured or not, so they run far above insurance payouts. How this is counted

Source: FEMA — National Risk Index (flood). Data: NRI December 2025 release; retrieved November 9, 2026.

Do the same homes flood again here?

Yes: FEMA's disaster-aid records hold 2,444 damage records from homes here that flooded more than once; 62 records are from homes FEMA's disaster-aid data flags as severe repeat-loss (SRL).

  • Repeat-flood damage records2,444
  • Records from homes flagged severe repeat-loss (SRL)62
  • Records in this state with no usable county code, not counted above5

These count damage events on repeat-flooded homes, not distinct homes. How this is counted

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Individual Assistance Multiple-Loss Flood Properties. Data: FEMA's current multiple-loss list; retrieved November 9, 2026.

How often is this county a flood disaster?

24 federal disasters for floods or storms here; the latest was Hurricane Milton (2024).

  • October 2024 — Hurricane Milton
  • September 2024 — Hurricane Helene
  • August 2024 — Hurricane Debby
  • August 2023 — Hurricane Idalia
  • November 2022 — Hurricane Nicole
  • September 2022 — Hurricane Ian

Only the latest are listed, newest first; disasters with the same month and title share one line, which says how many; the count covers every flood, hurricane, tropical-storm and coastal-storm declaration FEMA lists here, plus severe-storm declarations whose title names flooding, including emergency declarations. How this is counted

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Disaster Declarations Summaries. Data: declarations through 2024; retrieved November 9, 2026.

Did FEMA aid homeowners after floods and storms?

Yes: FEMA approved $175.1 million for homeowners here after floods and storms, about $1,648 per registration.

FEMA disaster aid helps with uninsured and underinsured losses, and is separate from NFIP insurance. The average is over every registration, including those approved for nothing. Only disasters counted in the flood-disaster card are included; their aid can still cover wind or tornado damage from the same storm. Disasters for COVID, fire, winter storms or tornadoes alone are left out.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Housing Assistance (Owners). Data: homeowner aid by disaster; retrieved November 9, 2026.

Are these counts complete?

Every record FEMA's download lists was received and counted.

In-force count: 60,758 policy units (from 38,940 API records; condo-association records carry more than one unit). Download check: policies: 38,940 of 38,940 fetched; claims: 13,688 of 13,688 fetched.
